title: Current status of bacteriophage therapy for severe bacterial infections
authors: Teiji Sawa, Kiyoshi Moriyama, Mao Kinoshita
text: This review describes bacteriophage therapy as a possible treatment option for severe infections caused by antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Bacteriophages are viruses that infect particular bacterial hosts, so treatment requires selecting phages that match the bacterium causing the infection. The review discusses reported clinical cases involving difficult-to-treat pathogens, including Acinetobacter and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. It also identifies limitations: narrow host range, the possibility that bacteria develop phage resistance, and the need to select and sometimes combine phages. Combining phages with antibiotics may improve outcomes in some cases. The article describes phage therapy as an emerging part of personalized medicine, while emphasizing that clinical development and careful selection remain important.

title: Personalized bacteriophage therapy outcomes for 100 consecutive cases: a multicentre, multinational, retrospective observational study
text: This retrospective observational study analysed the first 100 consecutive cases of personalized bacteriophage therapy for difficult-to-treat infections, reported through a Belgian consortium involving hospitals in multiple countries. The infections commonly involved the lower respiratory tract, skin and soft tissue, or bone. The researchers described individually selected phages and defined phage cocktails directed at the bacterial pathogens. They reported clinical improvement in 77.2 percent of infections and eradication of the targeted bacteria in 61.3 percent. In this dataset, bacterial eradication was less likely when concomitant antibiotics were not used. The study also documented phage resistance in some cases and phage-antibiotic synergy in evaluated patients. These findings are observational and should not be interpreted as proof of efficacy for every patient or infection.

title: A blueprint for broadly effective bacteriophage-antibiotic cocktails against bacterial infections
text: This study proposes a strategy for designing phage-antibiotic combinations using groups of bacteriophages that recognize non-redundant bacterial receptors. The authors describe screening for complementary phage groups to create cocktails with broader activity and to reduce the emergence of bacterial resistance. They report that selected combinations acted against a large proportion of tested Pseudomonas aeruginosa clinical isolates, including biofilm cultures, and were also evaluated in an in vivo wound infection model. The work further examines interactions between phage groups and antibiotic classes, as well as combinations targeting Staphylococcus aureus and mixed bacterial cultures. The results provide a research approach for developing broader phage-based treatments, but they do not establish a universal cocktail for all bacterial infections.

title: Phage therapy: A novel approach against multidrug-resistant pathogens
text: This review discusses bacteriophage therapy as an alternative research and treatment approach for infections involving multidrug-resistant bacteria. Lytic bacteriophages attach to susceptible bacterial hosts, replicate, and can cause bacterial cell lysis. The article reviews phage biology and different therapeutic strategies, including conventional phages, modified phages, phage-derived enzymes, and combination approaches. It notes that specificity is an advantage because phages can target particular bacteria, but narrow host range creates a need to match phages with the infecting pathogen. Important translational challenges include phage resistance, safety, immune responses, regulatory requirements, manufacturing, and the absence of standardized treatment protocols. The review argues that future work must improve effectiveness and safety before broader clinical integration.

title: A Comprehensive Review on Phage Therapy and Phage-Based Drug Development
text: This open-access review surveys the renewed interest in bacteriophages as potential tools against multidrug-resistant bacteria. It discusses the history and modern development of phage therapy, mechanisms by which phages infect and lyse bacterial cells, and possible applications against infections involving biofilms and intracellular pathogens. It also considers phage-based therapeutic development and the research needed to translate laboratory findings into clinical use. For a literature retrieval system, this paper is relevant to searches about phage mechanisms, antimicrobial resistance, biofilm-associated infection, and phage-derived therapeutic products. This record is a short paraphrased summary of the article abstract and bibliographic description, not a substitute for reading the full article.

title: Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2024
authors: Guangzhi Xiong, Qiao Jin, Zhiyong Lu, Aidong Zhang
text: Xiong and colleagues present MIRAGE, a benchmark for evaluating retrieval-augmented generation in medical question answering. The benchmark contains 7,663 questions across five medical QA datasets and compares combinations of corpora, retrievers and language models. The study discusses the importance of retrieval configuration, evidence placement and the lost-in-the-middle effect. It informs the evaluation design for LYSIS; it does not demonstrate that an LLM or medical RAG generation stage has been implemented in this project.

title: MedCPT: Contrastive Pre-trained Transformers with Large-scale PubMed Search Logs for Zero-shot Biomedical Information Retrieval
authors: Qiao Jin, Won Kim, Qingyu Chen, Donald C. Comeau, Lana Yeganova, W. John Wilbur, Zhiyong Lu
text: Jin and colleagues introduce MedCPT, a contrastively pretrained pair of biomedical retrieval encoders and a reranker trained using large-scale PubMed search logs. The paper reports zero-shot biomedical information retrieval evaluations. MedCPT is a candidate future upgrade for LYSIS, but the present implementation uses an NumPy-based TF-IDF and truncated-SVD LSA index; MedCPT model weights and inference are not integrated.

title: Phage-antibiotic combinations against multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa in in vitro static and dynamic biofilm models
text: Holger and colleagues evaluate phage-antibiotic combinations against multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa in static and dynamic in-vitro biofilm models. The study reports that selected multi-phage combinations with antibiotics reduced biofilm burden in the tested models, and that adding a phage to the cocktail could help limit resistance to component phages. The work is relevant to LYSIS literature retrieval for queries about Pseudomonas, MDR isolates, biofilm models, phage cocktails and antibiotic combination evidence. These are laboratory model findings and should not be generalized to clinical treatment outcomes.

title: Targeting Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilm with an evolutionary trained bacteriophage cocktail exploiting phage resistance trade-offs
text: Kunisch and colleagues describe an in-vitro directed-evolution approach that trains bacteriophages against Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilms. The study reports expanded host spectrum, improved antimicrobial efficacy and enhanced antibiofilm performance for evolved phages. A two-phage cocktail is reported to improve antimicrobial efficacy while avoiding dual-phage resistance in the tested bacteria. This paper is particularly relevant to LYSIS searches about Pseudomonas biofilms, phage adaptation, resistance trade-offs and cocktail design; the findings are experimental and not a clinical decision rule.

title: The synergistic effect between phages and Ceftolozane/Tazobactam in Pseudomonas aeruginosa endotracheal tube biofilm
authors: Viviane de C. Oliveira et al.
text: Oliveira and colleagues test phages and ceftolozane/tazobactam against mature Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilms formed on endotracheal-tube surfaces. The study compares short- and longer-duration treatment combinations and reports strain-dependent effects. In the tested susceptible strains, combined or sequential phage-antibiotic exposure reduced biofilm viability more than some single-agent arms, whereas no antibiofilm activity was observed in the tested resistant strains. The results emphasize strain dependence and the need to avoid treating in-vitro synergy as universal.

title: Bacteriophages as potential antibiotic potentiators in cystic fibrosis: a new model to study antibiotics with a phage cocktail targeting dual-species biofilms
text: Wang and colleagues describe an in-vitro artificial-sputum model for studying antibiotic and phage-cocktail combinations against dual-species biofilms containing Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus. The work examines biomass and bacterial counts after treatment with antibiotics, phages and combinations. The reported effects differ between the two species and depend on the phage-antibiotic pairing, making this record relevant to LYSIS queries about cystic fibrosis, polymicrobial infection and mixed-species biofilms. The study is a laboratory model, not clinical outcome evidence.

title: Phage-antibiotic combinations to control Pseudomonas aeruginosa-Candida two-species biofilms
authors: Prasanth Manohar, Belinda Loh, Ramesh Nachimuthu, Sebastian Leptihn
text: Manohar and colleagues study phage-antibiotic and antifungal combinations in single- and dual-species biofilms involving Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Candida albicans. The study addresses polymicrobial biofilm conditions rather than a single bacterial species alone. It is relevant to LYSIS queries about Pseudomonas-Candida interactions, polymicrobial biofilms and combined antimicrobial approaches. The record should be interpreted as experimental biofilm research, not evidence of an approved treatment protocol.

title: Bacteriophage therapy against Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilms: a review
venue: Annals of Clinical Microbiology and Antimicrobials
text: Chegini and colleagues review research on bacteriophage therapy against Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilms. The review discusses biofilm-specific challenges and proposed phage-related antibiofilm mechanisms, providing background for interpreting experimental studies. It is useful for broad queries about phage-biofilm interactions and research gaps, but review-level discussion should be distinguished from primary experimental evidence.

title: Combinations of Bacteriophage Are Efficacious against Multidrug-Resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Enhance Sensitivity to Carbapenem Antibiotics
text: Kovacs and colleagues report on bacteriophages targeting a multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa strain and examine combinations with carbapenem antibiotics. The article reports enhanced bacterial killing for selected phage-antibiotic combinations compared with individual treatments in the experimental system. This record supports retrieval for Pseudomonas, MDR, carbapenem and phage-antibiotic combination topics. It does not provide patient-specific clinical advice or establish a general antibiotic regimen.

title: Bacteriophage-Antibiotic Combination Therapy against Pseudomonas aeruginosa
authors: Guillermo Santamaría-Corral, Abrar Senhaji-Kacha, Antonio Broncano-Lavado, Jaime Esteban, Meritxell García-Quintanilla
text: This review summarizes research on bacteriophage-antibiotic combinations against Pseudomonas aeruginosa, including in vitro and in vivo work and reported clinical applications. It discusses proposed synergistic interactions and the use of combinations in difficult-to-treat infections. The review is a synthesis of heterogeneous studies; results depend on the phage, bacterial strain, antibiotic and experimental context, and should not be treated as a universal treatment protocol.

title: Bacteriophage Therapy on an In Vitro Wound Model and Synergistic Effects in Combination with Beta-Lactam Antibiotics
authors: Guillermo Santamaría-Corral, John Jairo Aguilera-Correa, Jaime Esteban, Meritxell García-Quintanilla
text: This in vitro study evaluated a Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteriophage with beta-lactam antibiotics in a wound-model setting. The authors report reduced viability of mature biofilms from multidrug-resistant strains and suppression of bacterial growth under the tested laboratory conditions. These findings are preclinical and model-specific; they do not establish safety or effectiveness in human wound treatment.

title: Combination of phages and antibiotics with enhanced killing efficacy against dual-species bacterial communities in a three-dimensional lung epithelial model
authors: Ergun Akturk, Graça Pinto, Lisa Ostyn, Aurélie Crabbé, Luís D. R. Melo, Joana Azeredo, Tom Coenye
text: This study used a three-dimensional lung epithelial model containing a dual-species community of Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus. It investigated phage and antibiotic combinations and reported that treatment sequence influenced antibacterial activity; phage treatment followed by gentamicin eradicated P. aeruginosa from the modelled community, while phage followed by ciprofloxacin reduced it. These are model-specific experimental findings and cannot be directly generalized to patient treatment.

title: Phage-Antibiotic Combinations for Pseudomonas: Successes in the Clinic and In Vitro Tenuously Connected
text: This review examines phage-antibiotic combinations for Pseudomonas and highlights a translational gap between promising laboratory interactions and clinical outcomes. It discusses the diversity of in vitro methods used to measure synergy and the difficulty of mapping measures such as plaque size or phage yield to meaningful treatment outcomes. The authors emphasize the need for standardized assays and reporting, and caution that laboratory synergy does not automatically predict clinical benefit.

title: Phage therapy against Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilm infections: challenges and advanced strategies
authors: Qianhe Xu, Shaoping Liu, Juan Xi
text: This 2026 review discusses barriers to phage therapy for Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilm infections. It groups challenges around biofilm and bacterial defenses, phage ecology, host pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics, and manufacturing and regulation. It describes how extracellular matrix composition, receptor accessibility, spatial structure, resistance and cocktail interactions can affect phage activity. It also notes that phage-antibiotic interactions may be synergistic or antagonistic depending on strain, dose and timing, and that AI/ML applications remain constrained by data quality. This is a review of research challenges, not a validated clinical algorithm.
